result.target_topic: Capital Conservation and Stress Capital Buffer Requirements
result.target_summary: Goldman Sachs calculates risk-based capital ratios under Standardized and Advanced Capital Rules, which include minimum requirements and additional conservation buffers composed primarily of Common Equity Tier 1 capital; failure to meet these constraints capital distributions and compensation. The stress capital buffer (SCB) reflects stressed losses from CCAR, includes planned dividends, and has a 2.5% floor, with the FRB approving capital distributions if a BHC must resubmit its capital plan.

Both disclosures concern the U.S. regulatory capital framework for Goldman Sachs and GS Bank USA as Category I/Advanced approach banking organizations. D074 establishes their Category I status and Advanced approach designation under the Capital Framework (Basel III/Dodd-Frank). D083 details the specific implementation of these standards, including the calculation of risk-based capital ratios under Standardized and Advanced Capital Rules and the associated conservation buffers. They share the same specific subject of the entity's capital requirement regime.

current_disclosures.summary: The Firm and GS Bank USA are subject to Category I risk-based regulatory capital and leverage requirements based on Basel III and the Dodd-Frank Act, involving quantitative measures and qualitative regulatory judgments, along with U.S. federal liquidity requirements.

target_year_over_year_context.explanation:
Both disclosures describe the calculation of risk-based capital ratios by Group Inc. and GS Bank USA under Standardized and Advanced Capital Rules, including minimum requirements and CET1 buffer constraints.

Both disclosures detail the consequences of failing to satisfy capital buffer requirements, specifically constraints on capital distributions and discretionary executive compensation based on eligible retained income.

2024 D083 establishes the regulatory capital framework for Group Inc. and GS Bank USA. 2025 D090 states that capital requirements for subsidiaries (GSBE, GSI, GSIB) include minimums and buffers and refers to MD&A. While D083 focuses on the Parent/GS Bank USA, it sets the context for the entire group's regulatory capital regime. D090 is a general disclosure about subsidiary capital requirements within that same Item 1 Regulation section. This is a supported link.

current_disclosures.summary: As Advanced approach banking organizations, Group Inc. and GS Bank USA calculate risk-based capital ratios using both Standardized and Advanced Capital Rules, which include minimum requirements and additional capital conservation buffer requirements satisfiable solely with Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital.

Failure to fully satisfy capital buffer requirements results in constraints on capital distributions and discretionary executive compensation, with severity depending on the shortfall amount and the organization's eligible retained income.
Capital requirements for GSBE, GSI, and GSIB include both minimum requirements and buffers, with detailed capital ratio information available in the MD&A and Note 20.

comparisons.peer_topic: Regulatory capital buffers impact on capital returns
comparisons.peer_summary: The Company's ability to pay dividends and repurchase stock is constrained by regulatory capital requirements, specifically the Stress Capital Buffer (SCB) and G-SIB surcharge, which increased to 3.2% and 3.0% respectively in 2024, potentially reducing shareholder returns.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs and Bank of America disclose that failure to meet capital buffer requirements results in constraints on capital distributions. GS specifically cites constraints on 'capital distributions and discretionary executive compensation' if buffer requirements are not satisfied. Similarly, BAC states that its 'ability to pay dividends and make common stock repurchases depends in part on our ability to maintain regulatory capital levels above minimum requirements plus buffers.' BAC further details that increases in the SCB directly decrease returns of capital, whereas GS details the mechanical constraint triggered by buffer shortfalls.

sentences.text: Failure to satisfy a buffer requirement in full would result in constraints on capital distributions and discretionary executive compensation.

The SCB reflects stressed losses estimated under the supervisory severely adverse scenario of the CCAR stress tests, as calculated by the FRB, and includes four quarters of planned common stock dividends.

Our ability to pay dividends and make common stock repurchases depends in part on our ability to maintain regulatory capital levels above minimum requirements plus buffers and non-capital standards established under the FDICIA.

To the extent that the Federal Reserve increases our stress capital buffer (SCB), global systemically important bank (G-SIB) surcharge or countercyclical capital buffer, our returns of capital to shareholders, including dividends and common stock repurchases, could decrease.

comparisons.peer_topic: CCAR Stress Testing and SCB Requirements
comparisons.peer_summary: JPMorgan Chase is subject to annual supervisory stress tests under the CCAR framework and must submit an annual capital plan, with the Federal Reserve using severely adverse scenario results to determine the Stress Capital Buffer (SCB); the firm is required to file its 2025 CCAR submission by April 5, 2025, with final SCB requirements effective October 1, 2025, amid pending changes to the framework and legal challenges.
comparisons.comparison: Both GS and JPM describe the Stress Capital Buffer (SCB) as being derived from the Federal Reserve's supervisory stress tests under the CCAR framework. GS states the 'SCB reflects stressed losses estimated under the supervisory severely adverse scenario of the CCAR stress tests.' JPM mirrors this, stating 'The Federal Reserve uses the results under the severely adverse scenario from its supervisory stress test to determine the Firm's Stress Capital Buffer ("SCB") requirement.' Both firms are subject to the CCAR framework and must submit annual capital plans to the Fed.

sentences.text: The SCB reflects stressed losses estimated under the supervisory severely adverse scenario of the CCAR stress tests, as calculated by the FRB, and includes four quarters of planned common stock dividends.

The SCB rule requires a BHC to receive the FRB's approval for any dividend, stock repurchase or other capital distribution, other than a capital distribution on a newly issued capital instrument, if the BHC is required to resubmit its capital plan, which may occur if the BHC determines there has been or will be a "material change" in its risk profile, financial condition or corporate structure since the plan was last submitted, or if the FRB directs the BHC to revise and resubmit its capital plan.

As a large BHC, JPMorganChase is subject to supervisory stress testing administered by the Federal Reserve as part of the Federal Reserve's annual Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review ("CCAR") framework.

The Federal Reserve uses the results under the severely adverse scenario from its supervisory stress test to determine the Firm's Stress Capital Buffer ("SCB") requirement for the coming year, which forms part of the Firm's applicable capital buffers.

comparisons.peer_topic: Regulatory Oversight, Activity Limits, and Prudential Standards
comparisons.peer_summary: Morgan Stanley operates as a bank holding company and financial holding company subject to comprehensive consolidated supervision by the Federal Reserve, with the CFPB overseeing consumer protection. The BHC Act limits permitted activities, requiring Fed approval for certain actions and providing a grandfather exemption for commodities trading, while the Volcker Rule prohibits proprietary trading and certain fund investments. Capital requirements are established by the Fed and OCC based on Basel III standards, with proposed comprehensive revisions pending. The firm is subject to capital planning, stress tests, and potential dividend restrictions. Liquidity standards include the LCR and NSFR, and as a G-SIB, the firm faces single-counterparty credit limits and additional prudential standards such as limits on short-term debt and early remediation frameworks.
comparisons.comparison: MS and GS both operate as large Bank Holding Companies (BHCs) subject to Federal Reserve capital requirements and stress testing frameworks that impact capital distributions. MS notes that Federal Reserve restrictions on capital distributions for large BHCs could affect its ability to pay dividends or repurchase stock. GS explicitly links its capital conservation buffers to constraints on capital distributions and executive compensation, and requires FRB approval for capital distributions if a BHC must resubmit its capital plan due to material changes or FRB direction. Both disclose the linkage between regulatory capital rules (Basel III/CCAR) and the ability to return capital to shareholders.

sentences.text: Both the Standardized and Advanced Capital Rules include minimum risk-based capital requirements and additional capital conservation buffer requirements that must be satisfied solely with Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital.

The SCB rule requires a BHC to receive the FRB's approval for any dividend, stock repurchase or other capital distribution, other than a capital distribution on a newly issued capital instrument, if the BHC is required to resubmit its capital plan, which may occur if the BHC determines there has been or will be a "material change" in its risk profile, financial condition or corporate structure since the plan was last submitted, or if the FRB directs the BHC to revise and resubmit its capital plan.

The Federal Reserve establishes capital requirements largely based on the Basel III capital standards established by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision ("Basel Committee"), including well-capitalized standards, for large BHCs and evaluates our compliance with such requirements.

For information about the Federal Reserve's restrictions on capital distributions for large BHCs, see "Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations-Liquidity and Capital Resources-Regulatory Requirements-Capital Plans, Stress Tests and the Stress Capital Buffer." All of these policies and other requirements could affect our ability to pay dividends and/or repurchase stock or require us to provide capital assistance to our U.S. Bank Subsidiaries under circumstances that we would not otherwise decide to do.
